marble.name: Experimental probability
marble.subject: Mathematics
marble.description: Record, describe, and analyse the frequency of outcomes from probability experiments to develop an understanding of relative frequency as an estimate of probability
marble.prompt: If you rolls a die 60 times and records the results, can they compare how often each number came up with what they'd expect in theory — and explain why they might not match perfectly?

misconceptions: Reporting the theoretical probability when asked for the experimental one, even for a biased/unknown device that has no calculable value
Concluding a device is biased (or fair) from too few trials (law of small numbers)
Thinking absolute counts must even out exactly with more trials (the 'due' fallacy) rather than relative frequency converging
Treating a small-sample relative frequency as a reliable estimate of the true probability
representations: Frequency table with a relative-frequency (f ÷ n) column
Relative-frequency graph stabilising as trials increase
Experimental and theoretical values marked on the same 0-to-1 scale
Biased/unknown device whose probability can only be estimated
authoredAnswer: A correct performance: records point-up/point-down in the table, computes relative frequency = point-up frequency ÷ 50, and offers THAT as the best estimate — recognising there is no theoretical value to calculate because the pin is not symmetric — while noting that 50 drops gives only a rough estimate and more trials would make it more reliable.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Gives 1/2 (or another symmetry-based value) instead of computing relative frequency from the drops
wrongAnswers.fix: Point out the pin is not symmetric, so there is nothing to calculate; the probability must be estimated from the data — relative frequency is the only route

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Declares the estimate settled after 50 drops with no caveat, or would judge fairness from a short run
wrongAnswers.fix: Show the relative frequency still shifting; extend trials or pool data so the estimate stabilises, and state that more trials give a more reliable estimate

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Expects point-up and point-down counts to become equal, or says a result is 'due'
wrongAnswers.fix: Distinguish relative frequency (stabilises toward the true probability) from raw counts (need not equalise); each drop is independent
